overview: The file centers on the National Geophysical Company’s December 1940 request for guidance before accepting a Nippon Mining Company commission to supervise geophysical exploration for petroleum in Japanese-ruled Formosa (Taiwan). It contains duplicate copies of the company’s inquiry, Commerce Department referral and acknowledgment memoranda, a State Department assessment—prepared after consultation with naval and military intelligence—that an American survey could provide useful information and prevent German engineers from obtaining the work, and a formal reply explaining the contemporary export-control position without guaranteeing future policy. Interfiled pages from January 1943 concern an unrelated Office of War Information request, the handling and authorship of a proposed historical response, and the proposed removal of an outdated quotation describing peoples as “uncivilized” or “civilized.”

subfiles.title: National Geophysical Company inquiry concerning oil exploration in Formosa
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce; copy to Department of State
subfiles.about: The company asks whether accepting a Japanese commission to supervise petroleum exploration in Formosa would accord with United States regulations and national obligations.
subfiles.summary: The National Geophysical Company reports an approach from the Nippon Mining Company of Tokyo concerning a multiyear geophysical exploration program intended to locate and produce oil in Formosa. It wishes to accept the work but seeks government guidance before doing so. The page bears an International Geophysical Company heading, although the body and signature identify the National Geophysical Company, and it was subsequently filed under 894A.6363/10.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on revising the OWI response
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Langdon; MHP)
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends removing a quotation from a 1900 legal memorandum and explains why Far Eastern Affairs should draft a historical reply.
subfiles.summary: Ward recommends omitting a quotation from the Solicitor’s memorandum of January 27, 1900 because the adjoining discussion characterizes peoples as “uncivilized” and “civilized” in a manner inconsistent with current policy. The memorandum also responds to questions about who should draft and sign the proposed reply. It argues that Far Eastern Affairs may appropriately prepare it because the issue is primarily historical rather than legal.

subfiles.title: Political Relations queries concerning an OWI information request
subfiles.about: The memorandum questions the purpose, drafting office, and proper signatory for a proposed response to an Office of War Information request.
subfiles.summary: The Adviser on Political Relations asks why the Office of War Information needs the material and how it relates to “Media Analysis and Language.” It also asks whether the legal office should draft the reply and, if Far Eastern Affairs does so, whether its chief or a secretarial officer should sign. The page forms part of the unrelated 1943 internal correspondence associated with pages 2 and 4.

subfiles.title: Draft communication to John Herrick and routing annotation
subfiles.from: M. J. McDermott, Chief, Division of Current Information
subfiles.to: John Herrick, Chief, Washington Office, Outpost Bureau, Office of War Information
subfiles.about: The page preserves the address and closing of a draft letter together with a note on the prescribed channel for communications with the Office of War Information.
subfiles.summary: This fragment identifies John Herrick as the intended recipient and M. J. McDermott as the proposed signatory. An annotation by J. C. states that communications of this kind should be handled through Herrick and McDermott under the current arrangement. It is evidently an underlying routing or draft page discussed in the January 25 and January 30 memoranda.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs assessment of the proposed Taiwan oil survey
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Coville; JPS)
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates the intelligence value and commercial implications of allowing an American company to conduct the proposed oil survey in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs records that both the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Military Intelligence Division considered an American survey desirable because it could yield information about Taiwan. Officials believed German engineers would probably undertake the work if an American company declined it. Neither the intelligence offices, the State Department, nor Commerce yet had information about the National Geophysical Company; Commerce was seeking a district-office report, and the memorandum suggests consulting Walden of a large oil company.

subfiles.title: Commercial Affairs routing note on the Commerce referral
subfiles.from: W. H. G., Bureau of Commercial Affairs
subfiles.about: A brief internal note records that Commerce sent the National Geophysical Company letter to the State Department for action and reply.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau of Commercial Affairs notes that the letter was received from the Department of Commerce. It assigns responsibility to the State Department for taking action and preparing the response.

subfiles.title: Commerce referral of the National Geophysical Company inquiry
subfiles.from: John F. Sinnott, District Manager, New York
subfiles.to: Metals and Minerals Division, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: The New York district office forwards John M. Templeton’s inquiry for central action and notes that it has not replied independently.
subfiles.summary: Sinnott forwards the original December 26 letter from the National Geophysical Company, described as a Dallas concern, and requests prompt attention. He notes that his office has neither answered the company nor otherwise acted. Although Templeton indicated that a copy had gone directly to State, Sinnott expects the State Department to answer the enclosed original; stamps document its subsequent referral and processing.

subfiles.title: Original National Geophysical Company letter concerning Formosa
subfiles.from: John M. Templeton, Vice President, National Geophysical Company
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce; copy to Department of State
subfiles.about: Templeton requests an official statement of American policy toward the company’s possible supervision of Japanese oil exploration in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Templeton says the Nippon Mining Company of Tokyo has asked the National Geophysical Company to supervise a long-term exploration program aimed at finding and producing oil in Formosa. The American firm would like the business but does not want to proceed unless it conforms to United States regulations and its perceived patriotic duty. This is the original enclosed version of the letter copied on page 1.

subfiles.title: Commerce acknowledgment and notice of referral to State
subfiles.from: W. A. Jansson, Chief, Metals and Minerals Division; forwarded by Robert Sovey
subfiles.about: Commerce acknowledges receipt of the company’s inquiry and reports that it has been referred to the State Department through the liaison officer.
subfiles.summary: Jansson acknowledges the New York office’s December 28 memorandum and its enclosed company letter. He states that the issue has been referred to the State Department for attention through Commerce’s liaison officer. Robert Sovey, Chief of the District Office Division, records its forwarding.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on export controls for oil-exploration equipment
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John M. Templeton, Vice President, National Geophysical Company
subfiles.about: The State Department explains the current export-control status of equipment needed for oil exploration and drilling while declining to predict future requirements or policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department recapitulates Templeton’s proposal to supervise Nippon Mining Company exploration in Formosa. It advises that equipment used to locate oil deposits and oil-well drilling machinery, except hydraulic pumps, was not then subject to export-license requirements. The Department nevertheless refuses to predict whether such equipment might later become controlled or what government policy toward actual exports would be if controls were imposed. The page is identified as a true copy of the signed original.

interest: The file is valuable for showing how a seemingly routine commercial inquiry became entangled with intelligence collection, export controls, and American strategic competition with Germany and Japan on the eve of the Pacific War. Particularly revealing is the candid judgment that an American survey of Taiwan could furnish useful information and that German engineers might otherwise take the contract. The duplicate company letters, routing slips, acknowledgments, internal assessment, and cautious final reply allow historians to reconstruct the bureaucratic path of the case. The apparently misfiled 1943 OWI papers are also useful evidence of State Department drafting practices and sensitivity to inherited colonial and racial language.
